name: Azerbaijani folk dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A master folk ensemble dancer rooted in traditional Azerbaijani choreography.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Dancing on Stone: The Living Traditions of Azerbaijan.
This is Azerbaijani folk dance. Ancient to modern.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (VlSeUtRN6g4)
Title card: Azerbaijani folk dance · Azerbaijan · Ancient to modern

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The process of formation for Azerbaijani national dances spans many centuries.
Archaeological evidence links modern practices to Mesolithic rock carvings of dancing people at Gobustan and Nakhchivan.
Early dances held ritual, heroic, and ceremonial characters.
on_screen: Map: Azerbaijan · Middle East
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dances are performed at weddings (such as Vagzali, Uzundara, and Anzali), Nowruz spring festivals (Banovsha, Bahar), agricultural and work celebrations (Choban Regsi, Mahsul), and martial or athletic displays (Zorkhana, Gangi).
They symbolize hospitality, unity, youthful enthusiasm, and the awakening of spring.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are divided into fluid, flowing, and lively rhythms.
Women's dances highlight smooth leg movements, elaborate hand gestures, shoulders, head positioning, and facial expressions.
Men's dances emphasize athletic footwork, including rising onto toes and rapidly dropping to the knees.
Watch for Yally circle movement.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (VlSeUtRN6g4)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circles, triangles, and lines; dancers holding hands or shoulders

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment relies on 6/8 and 3/4 time signatures.
Traditional instruments include the balaban, nagara drum, and dayereh (qaval).
Listen for the balaban, nagara, dayereh.
The pulse is 6/8 and 3/4.
Accompanied by traditional folk instruments like the balaban and nagara drum, featuring distinct 6/8 and 3/4 time signatures ranging from slow, doleful melodies to fiery, rapid rhythms.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear traditional Azerbaijani clothing, which is well-preserved through performance.
Women's costumes feature long skirts that shape footwork and colourful garments suited for festive gatherings like Nowruz spring celebrations and weddings.
on_screen: Image gallery: 6 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include choreographers and dancers Alibaba Abdullayev, Amina Dilbazi, Rosa Jalilova, Tutu Hamidova, Tanxo Izrailov, Afaq Melikova, and accordionist Teyyub Damirov.

Regional dances include Abayi and Agir Karadaghi from Shaki and Zagatala; Asta Karabagi from Karabakh; Qazakhi from the Qazakh District; and group Yally variants from Nakhchivan such as Kochari, Tenzere, and Sharur.
Rooted in ancient Caucasian folk traditions and ritual circle dances, with deep ties to regional Persian and Caucasian musical forms.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Proud head, upright posture.
Intricate hand movements, complex spins, and synchronized up-and-down arm movements in circle dances.

Clap it first, then step it in place.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Hold hands or shoulders in a circle for Yally formation.
Step 2: Execute synchronous rhythmic steps moving up and down.
Footwork from the sources: Women's leg movements are smooth, determined by skirt length; men's footwork includes rising on toes and quick knee drops.
Drill: Hand-in-hand circle holding.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); three repetitions of every step before moving on
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Perform graceful hand and upper-body movements for women's dances.
Step 4: Execute athletic footwork featuring toe rises and quick knee drops for men's dances.
Drill: Synchronous up-and-down stepping.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Basic rhythm keeping to 6/8 meter.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

music_brief.purpose: copyright-free soundtrack with the same DNA as the tradition's music — an original creation, not a reproduction
music_brief.sound_description: Accompanied by traditional folk instruments like the balaban and nagara drum, featuring distinct 6/8 and 3/4 time signatures ranging from slow, doleful melodies to fiery, rapid rhythms.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Azerbaijani folk dance (Azerbaijan). Meter 6/8 and 3/4. Instruments: balaban, nagara, dayereh. Mood: quick, slow, dynamic, lyrical, energetic. It should sound like this: Accompanied by traditional folk instruments like the balaban and nagara drum, featuring distinct 6/8 and 3/4 time signatures ranging from slow, doleful melodies to fiery, rapid rhythms. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
